guides.title: Your first Planning Poker session with StoryFlop
guides.description: Prepare a story, assign roles and follow a complete round from private votes to a team decision.

sections.title: 1. Bring a story the team can discuss
paragraphs: Before opening the room, write the user's outcome and how to verify it. “Improve access” is vague; recovery through an expiring email link describes a concrete behaviour.

Practise with password recovery and an existing email service. The link expires, works once and explains invalid links clearly. Changing provider is excluded. This fictional estimate is not a universal reference.
Bring a completed story the team knows to compare relative size, including tests and review. If work is unclear or a missing decision changes scope, note the question before voting.

sections.title: 2. Create the room and agree who does what
paragraphs: On the homepage, choose Create room, enter the session name, your name and an avatar. Share the link or code. Everyone joins from a browser without registering.
The organiser runs rounds and reveals votes. Collaborators can help with stories and rounds. Estimators vote; others may observe. Check roles before starting.
Add the story's title, description and optional task link. Share only authorised information and keep lasting decisions in your work system: rooms are temporary.

sections.title: 3. Clarify scope and vote without announcing a number
paragraphs: Read the story and ask about email availability, link reuse and expiry messages. Once scope is shared, open the round and choose cards independently.
StoryFlop offers 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 and 34, plus ? and a break. Values compare work within the team, not fixed hours. Use ? for missing information.
Wait for voters before revealing. Announcing “I think it's a 5” influences others. Private voting preserves different perspectives until discussion.

sections.title: 4. Reveal, discuss and record the decision
paragraphs: Suppose votes are 3, 5 and 13. Ask what each person included. Here, 13 assumed building the email service; 3 omitted expiry tests. Cards expose those differences.
Clarify that email exists and tests are included. Vote again if understanding changes. This team may agree on 5; other teams with different references may choose differently.
Record the final estimate and assumptions. Without agreement, split the story or investigate a concrete question. The average describes votes, not the agreed scope.

sections.title: 5. Finish with a useful check
paragraphs: Ask what was discovered that was not written down and add it to the task. A session should produce a clearer story as well as a number.
Transfer needed decisions from history to the backlog. Rooms and data are deleted after 14 days of inactivity. Keep useful references and review outdated ones for the next session.
Planning Poker is a technique for your context. The Scrum Guide does not require cards or story points. Adapt sessions to understand work rather than voting without purpose.

sources.label: James Grenning: Planning Poker, the original paper
Scrum Guide: Product Backlog and refinement

guides.title: Votes of 3, 5 and 13: resolving disagreement
guides.description: A password-recovery case to distinguish differences in scope, uncertainty and team references.

sections.title: The case: one sentence, three different jobs
paragraphs: “Allow password recovery by email.” In this fictional case, Ana votes 3, Bruno 5 and Cris 13. Mean 7 and median 5 explain neither person's understanding.

Ana assumes a reusable screen and existing email. Bruno includes expired-link handling and tests. Cris includes selecting and integrating a provider. Another vote without clarification repeats the issue.
Facilitation uncovers what estimates contain. Rather than “Why so high?”, which can pressure someone to lower a vote, ask which steps and risks were included.

sections.title: Three questions that turn numbers into information
paragraphs: First, ask what already exists. Review components, permissions, services and data. Confirming the email service removes a major scope difference.
Second, ask what must happen to finish the story. Specify expiry, single use and clear messages. A screen-only estimate differs from one including these checks.
Third, ask what is unknown and how to learn it. If invalidating links is unclear, assign a bounded investigation rather than hiding uncertainty behind a precise number.
checklist: What exists and can be reused
What the team's Definition of Done includes
What is unknown and who will clarify it

sections.title: Choose whether to clarify, split or investigate
paragraphs: Clarify when interpretations differ. Confirm the existing service and add tests to the description so everyone re-estimates the same work.

Split separable useful outcomes: email recovery for existing accounts could precede another channel if each meets quality criteria. Separating coding from testing does not itself reduce delivery size.
Investigate technical or product questions that prevent sensible estimation. Define evidence, an owner and a review time. Investigation should enable a decision, not postpone the story indefinitely.

sections.title: Repeat when new information appears
paragraphs: After clarifying, choose cards privately again. Votes of 5, 5 and 5 suggest closer understanding, not a guarantee against implementation surprises.
If votes become 5, 5 and 8, check remaining assumptions. Do not repeat until someone gives in. Agree how to proceed, document risks or split again.
Use distribution and history in StoryFlop to recall the discussion. Do not automatically adopt the mean: it can fall between cards and is not a shared decision.

sections.title: What to write in the task afterwards
paragraphs: Illustrative note: existing email; single-use link, expiry and error tests included; provider replacement excluded; agreed estimate 5; review if the service changes. It is not a universal estimate.
Using points to compare individuals or demanding identical initial votes removes useful information. Differences uncover hidden work and support decisions.
If questions recur next session, add them to preparation. A concrete process improvement matters more than matching cards.

sources.label: James Grenning: Planning Poker's origin and purpose

guides.title: User stories ready to estimate
guides.description: Three worked examples to uncover scope, tests and dependencies before choosing a card.

sections.title: Preparation does not mean knowing every detail
paragraphs: A story ready for discussion has an understandable outcome, boundaries and visible questions, not an exhaustive specification. Refinement clarifies and breaks down work as you learn.
These fictional exercises have no preset points. Size depends on product, dependencies, quality practices and team references. Start by explaining the intended delivery.
This preparation aid is not an official Scrum rule or a barrier to discussing uncertainty. A better question is useful even when you cannot estimate yet.

sections.title: Example 1: find orders by reference
paragraphs: A support person finds an order by full reference. The API and reusable search field exist. Partial matches and new filters are excluded.
Acceptance: valid reference shows an authorised order; unknown reference shows an empty state; network error permits retry without losing text. Search has a clear label and works by keyboard.
Ask about permission checks, pasted spaces and API tests covering the screen's contract. If the API does not exist, the original scope has changed.
Compare with a similar completed search. Make new permission models explicit; visual similarity does not imply equal size.

sections.title: Example 2: turn off a summary email
paragraphs: An account holder can disable weekly summaries in preferences. Recovery emails remain enabled. Custom frequency is excluded.
Acceptance: settings persist across sign-ins, sending respects changes and save errors restore the previous state. Decide what happens to already queued summaries.
Uncertainty may be in sending, not the switch. Consult someone familiar with it; investigate unknown queue behaviour before estimating.
Start with a binary setting and leave extra frequencies for later. Each part must work end to end. A screen without sending changes only appears functional.

sections.title: Example 3: export report results
paragraphs: An authorised user downloads filtered results as CSV, with agreed columns and readable headers. This fictional product story is not an announced StoryFlop feature.
Clarify volume, dates, special characters and permissions. Visible page or all filtered results? What appears while waiting? Answers may require different solutions.
Acceptance: matching filters, preserved accents, compatibility with the target tool and no unauthorised rows. Include security and safe handling of formula-like values.
Investigate uncertain volumes using representative authorised data. An explicitly limited useful export may be a first step rather than a full export with unknown cost.

sections.title: The shared check before voting
paragraphs: Ask two people to explain the story. Clarify differing outcomes. Include tests, review, permissions and dependencies in the work to finish.
Record exclusions to prevent recurring assumptions. Assign an owner and review time for questions that can change the solution substantially.
Keep answers in the template and bring the story's title and description to StoryFlop. Transfer the agreement to your backlog to preserve context for implementation.
checklist: We can explain the expected outcome
We know how to verify it
Dependencies, boundaries and questions are visible

guides.title: Split large stories without losing a useful outcome
guides.description: Three before-and-after cases to narrow complete deliveries, maintain quality and estimate again meaningfully.

sections.title: 1. Discover what makes the story large
paragraphs: A high card may expose many scenarios, unresolved dependencies or an unclear outcome. No point threshold requires every team to split. Ask which part you cannot explain or verify yet.

This guide uses a fictional reporting and ordering product. Its decisions illustrate possibilities, not observed StoryFlop customer results. Before splitting, write who needs the outcome and what the first delivery enables.

sections.title: 2. Keep a complete journey
paragraphs: Separating “build the API”, “make the screen” and “test” may organise tasks without producing three useful stories. Look for a narrow capability including the layers and checks needed to work.

Narrowing scope does not mean removing permissions, accessibility or tests to lower a number. If exporting data requires checking who may see it, include that protection in the first delivery. Constraints must be explicit and acceptable to its users.

sections.title: 3. Choose a constraint you can explain
paragraphs: Start with one format, channel, user type or business rule. Manual CSV and scheduled PDF exports address different needs. Confirm which enables value or learning first; do not split merely because screens look separate.

If data volume or provider behaviour is unknown, define an investigation with a question, owner and review. Its findings may change the split. Do not promise a limited delivery nobody can actually use.

sections.title: 4. Check the split before voting
paragraphs: For each part, describe a demonstration: who enters, what they do and what outcome they verify. Include an error case and access conditions. If showing anything requires three other unfinished stories, reconsider the split.

Re-estimate each story with the same team and references. Do not mechanically distribute original points: splitting can uncover shared work, remove assumptions or change the solution. The parts need not add up to the original estimate.

sections.title: 5. Keep the link to the original need
paragraphs: Record first-delivery scope, deferred work and reasons. Link back to the original need and state dependencies between parts. Revisit whether the constraint remains useful when priorities change.

Next session, ask whether the first part can be verified and supported a decision. If it only created unfinished work, adjust the pattern. Keep these assumptions beside estimates in the refinement template.

sources.label: Mountain Goat Software: splitting stories by outcomes

cases.title: Export reports
cases.before: “Export every report as CSV and PDF, with scheduling and all filters.” Volume and who can download each row are unclear.
cases.after: First story: manually download one report as CSV, with agreed columns, existing permissions, an explicit volume limit and testable errors. PDF and scheduling are later outcomes.
cases.decision: Choose one format and a complete journey while keeping access checks and tests. Validate that the volume limit still makes the delivery useful.

cases.title: Notification preferences
cases.before: “Configure every notification through email, mobile and in-app channels.” Different channels and rules are mixed.
cases.after: First story: disable the weekly email summary, persist the preference and verify that sending respects it. Essential access-recovery messages remain active.
cases.decision: The preference works end to end. Do not deliver a visual switch separately from sending. Prioritise other channels after confirming this need.

cases.title: View orders by role
cases.before: “A dashboard for every role and organisation, with search, export and administration.” Permissions and flows remain undefined.
cases.after: First story: a person views their orders under existing authorisation, with reference search and empty/error states. Cross-organisation administration and export are excluded.
cases.decision: Narrow the persona and journey without postponing authorisation. If the existing policy does not cover access, resolve that question before calling the story ready.

guides.title: Read the mean, median and distribution in StoryFlop
guides.description: Calculated examples to understand what votes describe and which decisions remain with the team.

sections.title: 1. Start with the cards, not the average
paragraphs: The distribution shows how many people chose each card. Before a summary number, check whether votes cluster, an extreme stands out or questions appear. The same average can hide very different conversations.
These fictional examples reproduce StoryFlop's calculation rules. Numbers help read results, not convert points to hours or compare individual or team performance.

sections.title: 2. Mean and median answer different questions
paragraphs: For 3, 5 and 13, the mean is 7: numeric votes added and divided by their count. The median is 5: the middle ordered value. The mean need not be a deck card.
Neither proves agreement. Ask what the 3 included and what the 13 saw. If they understood different work, clarifying scope matters more than choosing between 5 and 7.

sections.title: 3. An outlier deserves a question
paragraphs: For 5, 5, 5 and 21, the mean is 9 and median 5. The median describes the centre without removing information in the 21. That voter may know an overlooked dependency.
Ask about work and risk rather than requiring a defence of a number. If information changes shared scope, vote again; otherwise record an investigation or split.

sections.title: 4. Zero counts; questions are not numbers
paragraphs: For 0, 5 and ?, the numeric votes are 0 and 5, so mean and median are both 2.5. Zero participates. The ? stays in the distribution and asks for clarification; it is not zero.
With ? and ☕ there are no numeric votes, so no mean or median is available. Even identical special cards express a question or break, not an agreed work estimate.

sections.title: 5. Separate the summary from the final decision
paragraphs: Matching cards mean identical votes. A useful agreement also confirms scope, quality and assumptions. Record why a final estimate was chosen and review it when the story changes.
Use history to recall which information caused another round. Do not rank people by distance from the mean. Planning Poker should help understand work rather than reward conformity.

sources.label: James Grenning: discussion and independent estimation

guides.title: Facilitate remote sessions without forcing consensus
guides.description: Preparation, speaking turns and a complete case to turn remote voting into clear decisions.

sections.title: 1. Prepare the discussion and roles
paragraphs: Before sharing the link, select a few stories with outcomes, criteria and open questions. Confirm facilitator, voters and observers. Collaborators can help the organiser prepare stories and manage rounds.
Agree on an accessible voice or text channel and a reference story. Silence is not agreement. Provide an explicit way to request clarification or a break.

sections.title: 2. Protect the independence of the first vote
paragraphs: Read the story and resolve understanding questions before cards are chosen. Avoid announcing a reference number during voting. StoryFlop keeps votes private until revealed, and observers are not counted as voters.
Check that expected voters can participate before revealing. Disconnection or delay is not voluntary abstention. If participation changes, confirm it with the group and explain how to proceed.

sections.title: 3. Give turns to understand, not to persuade
paragraphs: After revealing, invite the lowest and highest voters to explain assumptions. Ask about existing components, included tests or unknown dependencies. Make room for risks not yet in the description.
If arguments repeat without information, summarise what is known. The next step may be clarification, splitting or investigation. Do not keep voting until someone changes their card through fatigue.

sections.title: 4. A remote case from start to finish
paragraphs: In this fictional exercise, three people estimate password recovery as 3, 5 and 13. The facilitator asks about email and tests. The team confirms the service exists and adds link expiry to the criteria.

The team votes again with clarified scope and agrees on 5 for this example. An unresolved question could instead end the session with an owner and next action, not a number. The template supports both outcomes.

sections.title: 5. Close with decisions you can retrieve
paragraphs: After each story, read out scope, estimate if any, risks and next action. Transfer them to the backlog. StoryFlop rooms and data are removed after 14 inactive days; history does not replace a lasting record.

At the end, ask which requirement was missing and whether everyone could participate. Use the answer for next time. Learning does not require publishing team information: public cases can be clearly identified fictional exercises.

sources.label: James Grenning: the purpose of independent voting
Scrum Guide: transparency and inspection of work

cases.title: From silence to a visible decision
cases.before: After 3, 5 and 13 are revealed, someone suggests “let's take 5” without asking the extremes. Two people remain silent and scope stays ambiguous.
cases.after: The facilitator assigns speaking turns, confirms existing email, includes tests and requests a new independent vote. Then the decision is read back and recorded in the task.
cases.decision: The important change is making assumptions and agreement visible. The 5 belongs to this exercise; it does not mean a real session must end with that number.

ui.threeGuides: Guides to prepare and facilitate your sessions
ui.takeTemplate: Take a refinement template with you
ui.takeTemplateBody: A worksheet for criteria, dependencies, votes and decisions. Includes a completed example and an editable version to copy, download or print.
ui.useResourcesBody: Start with the demo and first-session guide. If voting gets stuck, read the disagreement case. Prepare your backlog with the story examples and template.
ui.fictionNotice: These are fictional learning exercises. Numbers illustrate conversations, not universal estimates. Adapt the materials to your team's work.
ui.projectLink: Learn about the project and suggest a correction.
ui.prepareTemplate: Prepare your next session with the template
ui.createTeamRoom: Create a room with your team
ui.sourcesBody: The examples and StoryFlop instructions were written for this section. These sources provide context for the method and refinement:
ui.demoDescription: Try a fictional round: choose a card, reveal votes and see how clarifying scope changes an estimate.
ui.demoTitle: Try a round. Discover the conversation.
ui.demoLead: Choose a card, compare perspectives and estimate again with new information. No account or team meeting needed.
ui.simulation: This local simulation uses fictional characters and votes. It does not create a room, connect to other participants or keep your choices after you leave.
ui.practicingBody: Independent voting exposes differences. Revealing cards lets you ask what scope each person considered. Repeat when discussion adds information.
ui.realRoom: In a real room, everyone votes from their browser and the organiser manages rounds. This demo uses prepared characters and decisions to explain a case.
ui.firstGuide: Read how to prepare your first session
ui.taskBody: An account holder requests a password-change link. It expires, works once and displays clear error messages.
ui.scopeBody: The email service exists. Expiry and reuse tests are included. Changing provider is out of scope.
ui.beforeBody: Compare with a familiar team story. Consider your assumptions about email and tests.
ui.revealedBody: The cards are revealed. You can compare votes now.
ui.hiddenBody: The characters have voted. Their cards stay hidden until you reveal the round.
ui.calculation: Calculations include your vote and exclude ? and ☕ from mean and median. Matching cards do not prove a shared understanding of scope.
ui.anaReason: Assumed a reusable screen and omitted expiry tests.
ui.brunoReason: Included the screen, single-use link and tests.
ui.crisReason: Assumed the email service needed building.
ui.discussBody: The team confirms existing email and includes tests. Would this information change your vote?
ui.agreed: The votes match; document the agreement
ui.stopDiscuss: Your card asks for a pause and discussion
ui.difference: Your difference is still useful information
ui.agreedBody: All four votes are 5. In a real session, confirm assumptions and record the agreed estimate.
ui.differenceBody: The characters voted 5, but your card differs. Explain the work or uncertainty you considered. The demo does not change your vote to force agreement.
ui.closingBody: Existing email service, single-use link, expiry and tests included. Provider replacement is excluded. The 5 is illustrative, not a recommendation for other teams.
ui.needsJs: Interaction needs JavaScript. The complete case can be read without it.
ui.templateDescription: Copy, edit, download or print a preparation and decision worksheet with instructions and a password-recovery example.
ui.templateTitle: Prepare the story. Keep the agreement.
ui.templateLead: A refinement template to bring useful questions and leave with more than a number.
ui.instruction1: Complete the expected outcome, criteria and dependencies before the session. Keep open questions visible.
ui.instruction2: Use one worksheet per story. Record assumptions behind the lowest and highest votes without unnecessary personal data.
ui.instruction3: After discussion, note whether to clarify, split, investigate or agree an estimate. Repeat if information changes.
ui.instruction4: Copy the agreement to your backlog. Keep the downloaded worksheet: this editor does not save changes.
ui.templatePermission: Copy and adapt this template for your team. It is not an official Scrum requirement or a substitute for discussion.
ui.editorBody: Adapt the fields before copying or downloading. Changes stay on this page and are lost when you close or reload it.
ui.copyFailed: Could not copy. Select the template text and copy it manually.
ui.templateNoJs: Select and copy the worksheet text. Enable JavaScript to edit, download or use the print button.
ui.exampleStoryBody: Recover access through an emailed link.
ui.exampleCriteriaBody: The link expires, works once and shows a clear error when invalid.
ui.exampleDependenciesBody: Existing email service. A new provider is excluded.
ui.exampleVotesBody: 3, 5 and 13. The 3 omitted expiry tests; the 13 included building email services.
ui.exampleInfoBody: We confirm the existing service and include testing.
ui.exampleDecisionBody: Repeat the round. This fictional team agrees on 5 and records clarified scope in its backlog.
ui.exampleReviewBody: Review scope and estimate if the available email service changes.
ui.missingInfoBody: Instead of forcing an estimate, record the question, owner and review time. For example: check invalidation of used links; assign an owner during the session; review before the next round.
ui.aboutDescription: Learn the project's purpose, who maintains it and how to report issues or suggest corrections.
ui.aboutTitle: A shared table to understand the work.
ui.aboutLead: StoryFlop is a free Planning Poker tool for teams estimating together in their browser.
ui.purposeBody: StoryFlop brings stories, private votes and results into a shared room. It helps teams discuss scope and uncertainty, with access by link and no participant registration.
ui.featuresBody: The organiser prepares stories, invites people and runs rounds. Participants vote or observe. History restores session context; reactions let people express themselves.
ui.retentionBody: Rooms are temporary: data is deleted after 14 days of inactivity. Keep decisions in your backlog and read the privacy policy before sharing information.
ui.ownerBody: StoryFlop is owned by Jaume Bonet Martín, providing the service as an individual. Identification details and terms are in the legal notice.
ui.authorship: Resources signed StoryFlop are project documentation and estimation exercises. They imply no certification or affiliation with the authors of the method or Scrum.
ui.editorialBody: Guides distinguish StoryFlop features from other product examples. Cases and characters are identified as fictional. Numbers explain decisions, not effort tables transferable between teams.
ui.correctionsBody: Each guide has a publication date and sources. Corrections and substantial changes will appear in content and review dates. Suggest improvements when instructions are unclear or outdated.
ui.contactBody: Email privacy.storyflop@gmail.com for application issues, guide corrections or privacy questions.
ui.reportBody: Include the page, browser and reproduction steps for an issue; link and paragraph for corrections. Do not send active room codes or confidential team content.
ui.landingDemoBody: Vote, reveal and see how clarifying scope changes an estimate, without creating rooms.
ui.landingGuidesBody: Your first session, resolving disagreements and three worked stories for backlog preparation.
ui.landingTemplateTitle: A template to take with you
ui.landingTemplateBody: Write criteria, questions and agreements. Copy, download or print your next session's worksheet.
ui.caseStudiesTitle: Worked cases: from initial scope to a decision
ui.labLead: Compare prepared examples. Calculations follow StoryFlop's rules; they do not decide for the team.
ui.labNote: Special cards appear in the distribution but not the mean or median. Zero does count. Matching cards are not a documented agreement.
ui.usageNotice: We measure aggregate resource usage without identifying visitors. We respect Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control.
